title: Scaraboid in form of hedgehog

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund and Edward S. Harkness Gift, 1920
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A tiny green stone object carved in the form of a hedgehog, with a rounded back and a small pointed snout. It is photographed large, but it is smaller than a fingernail.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, date, medium, period, dimensions, tags (Animals), public-domain flag, credit line and image URLs read from the record

context: A tiny carving from ancient Egypt in the form of a hedgehog, made some time between about 1981 and 1295 B.C. It is only about 8 millimeters long, which is smaller than a fingernail. Its title calls it a scaraboid, a type of small object related to the scarab seal.

descriptions.k: This is a tiny hedgehog carved from green stone. It is smaller than your fingernail! It has a round back and a little nose. It was made in Egypt a very long time ago. Can you imagine holding it?
descriptions.g12: This hedgehog is so small it would fit on the tip of your finger. A craftworker in ancient Egypt carved it from green stone more than 3,000 years ago. It has a rounded back and a pointed nose. Why might someone make a hedgehog this tiny?
descriptions.g35: This scaraboid is a tiny carving in the shape of a hedgehog, only about 8 millimeters long. It is made of steatite, a soft stone that can be carved easily and was often given a green glaze. Egyptians made small seal-like objects like this, and many have designs on their flat undersides. What does this miniature tell you about the skills of the person who made it?
descriptions.g68: Made sometime between about 1981 and 1295 B.C., this scaraboid shows the Egyptian love of miniature animals. Steatite is soft, so it can be shaped into fine forms, and the green glaze would have given it a bright finish. A scaraboid is related to the scarab, a beetle-shaped seal or amulet, but here the animal is a hedgehog. How does the artist suggest a hedgehog with such a tiny form?
descriptions.g910: This hedgehog scaraboid shows how much character Egyptian craftspeople could pack into an object smaller than a fingernail. Soft steatite allows precise carving, and the glaze adds color and a protective surface. Scarab-like objects often served as seals or amulets, and the base may carry a design, but the record does not describe one here. What does miniaturization demand of a maker, and what does it demand of a viewer?
descriptions.g1112: The hedgehog scaraboid raises questions about scale, function, and meaning. Its dimensions, about 8 mm long, imply handling at the level of the fingertip, and steatite's softness made such detailed carving possible. Scarabs and scaraboids served as seals and amulets in Egypt, but the record offers no inscription or context to show how this one was used. Thinking about it invites a discussion of how tiny objects carry value, how animals were chosen for such forms, and how museums enlarge things that were meant to be seen up close.

safety.method: Title, tags (Animals), medium (green glazed steatite) and period checked against the museum record. Subject is a tiny hedgehog carving with no people. The image file itself was not visually inspected in this build. A person should confirm it in the review tool before release.

teacherNote.context: A tiny glazed steatite scaraboid in the form of a hedgehog, about 8 mm long. Scarabs and scaraboids were used as seals and amulets in Egypt, but the record gives no use for this piece.
directions: Have students draw an animal at the size of a fingernail to feel the challenge of miniature work.
Ask students to explain why scale information is important when viewing museum photographs.
Discuss how soft stone makes detailed carving possible.
